passage:
"Sangeeta, you're coming, right? We're all bunking the last period to go to the lake."
"Um… yeah. Sure."
Later, by the lockers:
"Arohi, can I tell you something? I don't actually want to go."
"Then why did you say yes?"
"Because if I don't, they'll laugh and call me a goody-goody. And then they'll go without me every time."
"That's a real fear. I have it too."
"You do?"
"I also don't want to go. My mum would kill me, and honestly the lake gets scary at that end."
"So… what if we both say no? Together?"
"Okay. What do we say?"
"Something short. Like, 'Not today, we've got a project.'"
"'Not today, we've got a project.' Say it again."
"Not today, we've got a project."
They practised it twice, giggling. When Riya came back to check, Sangeeta said it first, steady, though her hands were cold. Arohi nodded beside her. Riya shrugged. "Your loss." And that was all.

qa.q: Where were the friends planning to go during the last period?
qa.a: To the lake.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta first say yes?
qa.a: She was afraid of being laughed at, called a goody-goody and left out of future plans.

qa.q: What helped Sangeeta say no, and why?
qa.a: Finding an ally in Arohi and practising a short reply together made it easier to refuse calmly.

qa.q: How does Riya react to the refusal?
qa.a: Riya just shrugs and says 'Your loss,' showing the feared reaction was much smaller than Sangeeta expected.

grounding: A teen who goes along out of fear of being left out admits the fear, finds an ally and practises a short reply.

Last year my friends started bunking Saturday tuition to hang around the arcade. The first week, I went. The second week too. I didn't even enjoy it. I kept checking the time and feeling guilty about the money Papa paid for tuition.
I went because I was scared. Scared they'd laugh, scared I'd be the one left out of every photo in the group.
One Saturday I noticed Yash was quiet too. On the walk, I asked him, "Do you actually want to be here?" He said, "Not at all." We both laughed, a bit shakily.
So we made a plan. We practised one line in his building's lift: "We're doing tuition today, see you after." Short. Boring. No speech.
The next Saturday we said it together. Someone called us nerds. That was it.
I'm Omkar, and what I learned is that fear doesn't disappear. It just gets smaller when someone stands next to you.

qa.a: To the arcade.

qa.q: Why did Omkar keep going along with the group?
qa.a: Omkar felt scared of being laughed at and left out, even while feeling guilty and not enjoying it.

grounding: A teen who goes along out of fear admits it, finds an ally who will say no too, and practises a short reply.

passage:
So, Preeti, you asked me why I changed. I'm Jatin, and here's the honest version.
In Class 9, I was the guy who did everything first. Bunking class, sneaking into the late movie, riding without a helmet. Anyone who said no, I called a baby. I said it to you too, remember? When you wouldn't bunk science.
I thought I was braver than everyone. Then one night, I got caught by my uncle, riding his scooter without a licence. He didn't shout. He asked, "Who are you trying to impress?"
That stuck. I realised I was terrified of looking weak. Calling others babies made me feel less scared. It was the same insecurity I mocked in them.
Now, if someone says no, I just say, "Cool." And when you went to science that day, you were the brave one.

qa.q: What did Jatin's uncle catch him doing?
qa.a: Riding his uncle's scooter without a licence.

qa.q: What was Jatin really feeling when he called others babies?
qa.a: He was insecure and terrified of looking weak, and mocking others made him feel less scared.

qa.q: What does Jatin do differently now, and why is it better?
qa.a: He simply says 'Cool' when someone says no, respecting different choices instead of pushing them into his risks.

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt when Jatin called her a baby for not bunking science?
qa.a: Preeti probably felt hurt and pressured, even though choosing to go to class took real courage.

grounding: A teen who called rule-following friends babies sees the same insecurity in himself and starts respecting their choices.

For three months I covered for Vikas. When his mother called asking where he was, I said, "He's studying with me." He was actually racing his cousin's motorbike on the highway at night with some older boys.
I thought that was what loyalty meant. You don't snitch. Friends protect each other.
Then one night he called me, laughing, saying they'd hit a hundred and ten on the flyover without helmets. I couldn't sleep. I kept seeing him on the road.
I asked myself: am I loyal to Vikas, or to his racing?
The next morning I told my father everything. He listened and said, "You're protecting him now, Deepak, not betraying him." He phoned Vikas's mother that afternoon.
Vikas didn't talk to me for a week. Then he did. He said, "I was angry. But I'd have been dead some night." We still hang out. Just not on the flyover.

qa.a: His cousin's motorbike.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel after Vikas's late-night call?
qa.a: Deepak felt frightened and sleepless, imagining Vikas hurt on the road.

qa.a: Deepak told his father, who called Vikas's mother the same day, because being loyal to Vikas's safety mattered more than covering the risky act.

I said, "Nope, not for me," and walked over to the bookshop. I wasn't trying to be a hero. My stomach was in knots.

Lalit met "Riya_travels" on a gaming site in September. She said she was sixteen, from Pune, and thought Lalit was "so mature for his age." They chatted every night.
Then last week she wrote: "Send me a photo of you, just you, no shirt. Our secret. Don't tell your parents, they won't get it."

Mohit beta, you've been so quiet since your mother's hospital visits started. Let me tell you about the year my father fell ill.
I was fifteen. Baba was in bed for months, and the shop was closed. At night I heard Amma whispering to my uncle about loans and fees. I didn't sleep. I thought I had to fix it all myself. I stopped meeting my friends so I could count money in secret.
The turning point came one night when Amma found me crying over the ration book. She sat down beside me. "Parul, beti, ask me. Don't guess in the dark."
So I asked. She told me, simply, what was happening and what the adults were doing about it.
Then she gave me small jobs: sorting the medicines box by day, helping my brother with homework. But she also said, "You still go to school. You still see your friends." I did.
Baba recovered slowly. And I learned: ask, help a little, and stay a child.

qa.a: Her uncle.

qa.q: How did young Parul feel when she heard the whispers?
qa.a: She felt anxious and afraid, unable to sleep, and believed she had to fix everything herself.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt finding Parul crying over the ration book?
qa.a: Amma probably felt sad and protective, realising her daughter was silently carrying worries meant for adults.

"Papa, what's happening with Mummy? Please tell me properly."

passage:
Hemant, you asked why I always said no to the birthday lunches last year. I'm Maria, and I'll tell you the truth now.
My father lost his job in April. Suddenly there was no money for anything extra. When everyone planned the café lunch for Anjali's birthday, I said I had tuition. For the class trip, I said my grandmother was ill. I made up so many excuses I started forgetting which ones I'd used.
The worst part was how ashamed I felt. Like being short of money made me less.
Once, I even thought about taking the money from Mum's purse, just to go once. I didn't. That scared me though.
Then in October I told Zoe, my best friend. Just her. She said, "Why didn't you say? We'll do a picnic at the park instead, everyone brings something." And she didn't make it weird.
Money isn't who I am. I know that now. I still say no sometimes. But I don't lie about why.

qa.q: When did Maria's father lose his job?
qa.a: In April.

qa.q: How did Maria feel about the family's money situation?
qa.a: Maria felt deeply ashamed, as if having less money made Maria less of a person.

qa.a: Telling one trusted friend and stopping the lies, which let friends adjust plans kindly and freed Maria from pretending.

qa.q: How does Zoe react when Maria tells her?
qa.a: Zoe is kind and practical, suggesting a picnic where everyone brings something, and doesn't make it awkward.

Sunday night
Ammi sat on my bed again tonight until one. She told me about the rent, about Abbu's medical reports, about what Khala said on the phone, about how she's scared all the time.
I'm proud she trusts me. I really am. She says, "You're the only one who understands, Abhinav." But when she leaves, my heart is pounding and I can't sleep. I have my chemistry test tomorrow and I haven't read anything.
Today in the kitchen I finally said it. "Ammi, I love you. I'll help with Abbu's medicines and the shopping. But the money and the doctors, can you talk about that with Khala or Farida Phuppo? I get too scared."
She looked at me for a long time. Then she hugged me and said, "You're right, jaan. I forgot you're still my child." She called Farida Phuppo right away.
I'm still worried. But tonight I might sleep.
